thesis: Maze of Ith turned a land slot into repeatable combat control, preventing damage while also untapping the attacker and creating timing decisions that ordinary removal never offered.

canonicalIdentity.currentOracleText: {T}: Untap target attacking creature. Prevent all combat damage that would be dealt to and dealt by that creature this turn.
canonicalIdentity.identityNotes: Original The Dark printing (August 1, 1994) and Anson Maddocks credit checked against the original printing record; current Oracle and 2022-12-08 rules checked against Wizards' Dominaria Remastered notes. Printed 1994 text must not be misrepresented as a modern Oracle transcription.

originalContext.setEnvironment: The Dark, released August 1, 1994; Anson Maddocks illustrated the original land. Maze has no mana ability.
originalContext.designPurpose: Interpretation of printed mechanics: a nonmana land slot buys repeated combat-damage prevention and untapping while the target stays attacking. No attributed designer intent is asserted.
originalContext.initialReception: No unsupported claim about 1994 contemporary reviews or immediate tournament adoption. Documented 2015 Old School deck registrations are treated as later examples.

loreContext.summary: The original artwork and the card's name suggest a dangerous place; no invented canonical story, named protagonist or depicted episode is asserted.

competitiveTimeline.significance: Maze of Ith appears as a land with a combat-damage prevention ability and no mana production.
Organizer-published list registers exactly one Maze of Ith in the 31-card business group, not its 29 mana sources. Opening story is fictional and does not recount Arce's play.

Dated official rulings confirm that an untapped vigilant attacker is a valid target, the creature remains attacking, the land provides no mana, and postdamage untapping does not reverse prior combat damage.

playbook.role: Repeatable combat damage control from a land card that cannot produce mana.
playbook.deckRequirements: Do not count Maze toward colored or generic mana production; build enough actual mana sources, and consider when single-target combat interaction is worth a full card slot.
playbook.copyCount: One Maze appears in Mark Arce's published 2015 mono-black 60-card list; other historical decks can play different counts.
playbook.mulligans: An opening hand containing Maze but insufficient mana-producing lands cannot rely on Maze to cast spells.
playbook.sequencing: The target is an attacking creature whether tapped or untapped. Use Maze before combat damage to prevent its combat damage; postdamage targeting can untap your own creature but does not reverse dealt damage.
playbook.sideboarding: Format- and matchup-specific; do not infer a mandatory plan from a single tournament registration.
playbook.commonMistakes: Claiming Maze removes an attacker, stops on-attack triggers, produces mana, or simultaneously prevents combat damage from an entire attack.

counterplay.directAnswers: Wasteland and other legal land removal, or Pithing Needle naming Maze of Ith; multiple attacking creatures dilute the value of a single activation.
counterplay.engineDisruption: Attack the supporting land tutor/recursion engine when Maze participates in a Lands strategy.
counterplay.timingWindows: Declare multiple threats; react to activated abilities when allowed, and recognize that an attack trigger has already occurred by the time Maze has an attacking target.
counterplay.racing: Damage from the un-Mazed attacker and noncombat sources still matters.
counterplay.sideboarding: Assess actual format legality and specific opposing threats rather than treating Maze as universal protection.

claims.summary: Maze of Ith was originally released in The Dark (August 1994), original artwork by Anson Maddocks; it is a land with no mana ability.

It can target an untapped attacker, does not remove it from combat, prevents only combat damage dealt by/to that target, and can untap one's own attacker after combat damage without undoing that damage.
Mark Arce's 2015 Old School Mono Black registration includes Maze of Ith, Hypnotic Specter, Swamp and the other black threats named in the reconstructed vignette.
Serra Angel, Kird Ape and Taiga are hypothetical opposing cards; neither a named opponent nor a played match for Arce is claimed. Combat and life-total arithmetic are reviewed under modern rules.
